sections.content:
You know *a menos que* from B1 Unit 21, *a no ser que* and *salvo que* from B2 Unit 9, and *excepto que* and *excepto si* from B2 Unit 11. Each one names the only thing that could stop the main clause from being true: *Iremos al campo a menos que llueva*. A useful test is to swap the phrase for *si no*: *Iremos al campo si no llueve* means the same.

The mood depends on the phrase. *A menos que*, *a no ser que*, *salvo que* and *excepto que* take the subjunctive, because the exception has not happened yet. *Salvo si* and *excepto si* are *si* phrases and take the indicative. After a past or conditional verb, the subjunctive is the imperfect.

sections.title: Same exception, two moods
rows: Iremos al campo a no ser que llueva.
We will go to the countryside unless it rains.
Iremos al campo, salvo si llueve.
We will go to the countryside, except if it rains.
Nadie entra, salvo que tenga permiso.
Nobody comes in, unless they have permission.
Dijo que vendría a menos que tuviera trabajo.
He said he would come unless he had work.

sections.content: The exception does not cancel the rule; it is the single case in which the rule would not hold. If you are not sure which mood to use, check the phrase: *que* means subjunctive, *si* means indicative.
